section_summary: The section concludes a Japanese election-law text with penalties, supplementary rules, and an annex listing electoral districts. It then contains a despatch about SCAP intelligence controls, five copies of the order at issue, and reports on Japanese party politics in March 1948. The final pages include the Democratic Liberal Party’s founding statements and the beginning of an abstract of its platform.

subfiles.title: Law for the Election of Members of the House of Representatives, concluding provisions and annex
subfiles.about: Concludes election offenses and procedures, lists electoral districts and member quotas, and gives transitional amendments.
subfiles.summary: The surviving text begins mid-article with punishments for election disturbances and continues through offenses involving weapons, fraudulent voting, campaign spending, and election administration. Supplementary articles address court proceedings and the transition to the new Constitution. A long annex lists electoral districts and their seat quotas across Japan. Final supplementary rules set the law’s commencement and amend related election and local-government laws.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 172, General Order No. 4, “Intelligence Targets in Japan”
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards SCAP’s intelligence order and raises concern that G-2 clearance could constrain the mission’s reporting.
subfiles.summary: Sebald says a literal reading of General Order No. 4 could require G-2 clearance for the mission’s reports to Washington. He recommends raising no immediate issue because of the mission’s working relationship with SCAP, while alerting the Department to the difficulty.

subfiles.title: General Orders No. 4, “Intelligence Targets in Japan” — copy 1
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Assigns G-2 responsibility for coordinating intelligence work and controlling document removal and outgoing reports.
subfiles.summary: The order rescinds earlier orders and gives the Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, coordinating control over intelligence collection in Japan. It covers technical material, documents, and military historical records. It requires clearance for removing Japanese records and for dispatching reports of possible intelligence value outside Japan.

subfiles.about: Second copy of the order coordinating intelligence collection through G-2.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate of General Orders No. 4, including G-2 clearance rules for Japanese documents and reports sent outside Japan.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 170, forwarding conversation with former Prime Minister Katayama
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards a memorandum explaining Katayama’s resignation and his opposition to Communist influence.
subfiles.summary: Forwards Katayama’s account of his Cabinet’s resignation and his plans to restore Socialist Party unity.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with former Prime Minister Katayama
subfiles.about: Records Katayama’s explanation of his resignation and discussion of socialism and communism.
subfiles.summary: Katayama says he resigned to prevent a split between right and left wings of the Social Democratic Party and intends to work on party discipline. He rejects cooperation with the Communists and discusses European anti-Communist measures with Sebald.

subfiles.title: Airgram A-738 quoting Manchester Guardian report on Japan
subfiles.about: Relays a newspaper account of an American economic mission and Japanese political developments.
subfiles.summary: The quoted article reports William Draper’s arrival with economic experts to study Japanese self-sufficiency. It also covers Ashida’s Diet address, the emergence of Yoshida’s new party, and Socialist rejection of a Communist people’s front.

subfiles.title: Airgram A-55 on inauguration of the Democratic Liberal Party
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the party’s formation, membership, leaders, and basic policies.
subfiles.summary: The Liberal Party dissolved on March 15 and a new Democratic Liberal Party was inaugurated with Yoshida as president. The report describes its Diet strength and its program for industrial rehabilitation, administrative reform, reduced controls, trade, tax reform, and labor-management cooperation. Page 502 is severely degraded in the OCR.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 208, inauguration of the Democratic Liberal Party
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Supplies party officer lists, Diet seat counts, and founding documents.
subfiles.summary: The despatch follows airgram A-55 with lists of party executives and consultants, Upper House appointments, and party strengths in both Diet houses. It encloses the new party’s declaration, statement of purpose, and platform abstract.

subfiles.title: Democratic Liberal Party declaration
subfiles.about: Declares the new party’s aims for democracy, production, rehabilitation, and international participation.
subfiles.summary: Rejects socialist ideology and bureaucracy while urging individual initiative, production, trade, and Japan’s reconstruction.

subfiles.title: Purpose of the Formation of the New Political Party
subfiles.about: Explains the rationale for a united democratic party and calls for public support.
subfiles.summary: Calls for democratic unity, production, industrial recovery, trade, and a responsible party under the new Constitution.

subfiles.title: Abstract of Tentative Platform of Liberal Party
subfiles.about: Begins an abstract of proposed policies on government, education, industry, agriculture, forestry, and fisheries.
subfiles.summary: Lists proposed democratic, economic, educational, transport, agricultural, forestry, and fishery policies; the abstract continues beyond this section.
